1	# SmolVLM: Redefining Small and Efficient Multimodal Models
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299
     5	
     6	## Overview
     7	
     8	SmolVLM is a family of compact vision-language models (VLMs) from Hugging Face and Stanford University, designed for resource-efficient inference on mobile and edge devices. The series includes three model sizes — 256M, 500M, and 2.2B parameters — that achieve competitive performance against much larger models while using dramatically less GPU memory. The smallest model, SmolVLM-256M, runs inference with less than 1GB GPU RAM and outperforms the 300× larger Idefics-80B model. All weights, datasets, code, and a mobile app (HuggingSnap) are fully open-sourced.
     9	
    10	## Architecture Design
    11	
    12	![SmolVLM Architecture](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    13	
    14	SmolVLM uses a pipeline where images are split into sub-images, encoded by a SigLIP vision encoder, compressed via pixel shuffle (space-to-depth), projected through a linear layer into the SmolLM2 language model's input space, and concatenated with text token embeddings. For video, frames are sampled and processed similarly.
    15	
    16	Three critical architectural findings drive the design:
    17	
    18	**Finding 1 — Balanced Encoder-LM Compute:** Compact VLMs benefit from smaller vision encoders. A 93M SigLIP-B/16 paired with a 135M LM outperforms a 428M SigLIP-SO400M with the same LM. Only at 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead.
    19	
    20	**Finding 2 — Extended Context Length:** Performance improves significantly when extending context from 2K to 16K tokens. This was achieved by increasing the RoPE base from 10K to 273K and fine-tuning on mixed long/short-context data. The 2.2B model uses 16K context; smaller variants use 8K.
    21	
    22	**Finding 3 — Aggressive Token Compression:** Pixel shuffle rearranges spatial features into channels, reducing visual tokens by r². While larger models use r=2, small VLMs benefit from r=4 (16× token reduction), easing attention overhead and improving long-context modeling.
    23	
    24	![Pixel Shuffle Diagram](./assets/figure_6.jpg)
    25	
    26	## Benchmark Performance
    27	
    28	SmolVLM was evaluated across 13 benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. The "Efficient OS" column shows the best open-source model under similar constraints.
    29	
    30	| Capability | Benchmark | SmolVLM 256M | SmolVLM 500M | SmolVLM 2.2B | Best Efficient OS |
    31	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    32	| Single-Image | OCRBench | 52.6% | 61.0% | 72.9% | 54.7% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    33	| Single-Image | AI2D | 46.4% | 59.2% | 70.0% | 71.0% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    34	| Single-Image | ChartQA | 55.6% | 62.8% | 68.7% | 48.0% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    35	| Single-Image | TextVQA | 50.2% | 60.2% | 73.0% | 61.5% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    36	| Single-Image | DocVQA | 58.3% | 70.5% | 80.0% | 77.7% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    37	| Single-Image | ScienceQA | 73.8% | 80.0% | 89.6% | 87.5% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    38	| Multi-task | MMMU | 29.0% | 33.7% | 42.0% | 33.9% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    39	| Multi-task | MathVista | 35.9% | 40.1% | 51.5% | 37.6% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    40	| Multi-task | MMStar | 34.6% | 38.3% | 46.0% | 43.1% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    41	| Video | Video-MME | 33.7% | 42.2% | 52.1% | 45.0% (InternVL2-2B) |
    42	| Video | MLVU | 40.6% | 47.3% | 55.2% | 48.2% (InternVL2-2B) |
    43	| **Average** | **All Benchmarks** | **44.0%** | **51.0%** | **59.8%** | — |
    44	
    45	**RAM Usage:** SmolVLM-256M uses 0.8 GB (batch=1), SmolVLM-500M uses 1.2 GB, and SmolVLM-2.2B uses 4.9 GB. For comparison, Molmo-A1B-7B requires 27.7 GB.
    46	
    47	## On-Device Deployment
    48	
    49	![Mobile App and Throughput](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    50	
    51	SmolVLM runs on-device via the HuggingSnap iOS app, processing photos and videos entirely locally with no cloud dependency. Throughput benchmarks across Apple Silicon devices show:
    52	
    53	- SmolVLM-256M achieves up to ~80 tokens/second on Pro M1 Max 64GB
    54	- At batch size 64, the 256M model reaches nearly 1000 tokens/second on high-end devices
    55	- Even on a MacBook Air M3 16GB, the 256M model produces ~55 tokens/second
    56	- Throughput scales roughly linearly with batch size for the smallest model
    57	
    58	## Key Findings
    59	
    60	- **Sub-1GB inference is achievable:** SmolVLM-256M uses only 0.8 GB GPU RAM at batch size 1, enabling deployment on smartphones and low-power edge devices.
    61	- **SmolVLM-256M surpasses the 300× larger Idefics-80B** despite an 18-month development gap, demonstrating that architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale.
    62	- **Balanced encoder-LM sizing, aggressive pixel shuffle (r=4), and extended context (up to 16K tokens)** are the three most impactful design choices for compact VLMs.
    63	- **SmolVLM-2.2B rivals state-of-the-art models** that consume twice the GPU memory, achieving 59.8% average across 13 benchmarks.
    64	- **All models, data, code, and a mobile app are fully open-sourced** to promote reproducibility and on-device AI research.

     7	## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist
     8	
     9	The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:
    10	
    11	| Banned Feature | Description |
    12	|----------------|-------------|
    13	| `clipPath` | Clipping paths |
    14	| `mask` | Masks |
    15	| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
    16	| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
    17	| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
    18	| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
    19	| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
    20	| `textPath` | Text along a path |
    21	| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
    22	| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
    23	| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
    24	| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
    25	| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |

    29	## 2. PPT Compatibility Alternatives

    34	| `<g opacity="0.2">...</g>` | Set `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity` on each child element individually |
    35	| `<image opacity="0.3"/>` | Overlay a `<rect fill="background-color" opacity="0.7"/>` mask layer after the image |

   107	
   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques
   109	
   110	> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).
   111	
   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.
   117	
   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```
   133	
   134	Recommended parameters:
   135	```
   136	stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2
   140	```
   141	
   142	#### Colored Shadow
   143	
   144	Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.
   145	
   146	```xml
   147	<filter id="colorShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   148	  <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="10"/>
   149	  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
   150	  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
   151	  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```
   158	
   159	Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.
   160	
   161	#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback
   162	
   163	Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:
   164	
   165	```xml
   166	<!-- Shadow layers (back to front, largest offset first) -->
   167	<rect x="68" y="72" width="400" height="240" rx="16" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
   168	<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
   169	<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
   170	<!-- Main card -->
   171	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
   172	```
   173	
   174	### Image Overlay
   175	
   176	#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common
   177	
   178	Best for: image+text pages. Gradient direction should match text position (text on left → gradient darkens toward left).
   179	
   180	```xml
   181	<image href="..." x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>
   182	<defs>
   183	  <linearGradient id="imgOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   184	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.85"/>
   185	    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
   186	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
   187	  </linearGradient>
   188	</defs>
   189	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
   190	```
   191	
   192	#### Bottom Gradient Bar
   193	
   194	Best for: cover slides and full-image pages with bottom title.
   195	
   196	```xml
   197	<defs>
   198	  <linearGradient id="bottomBar" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
   199	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   200	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.72"/>
   201	  </linearGradient>
   202	</defs>
   203	<rect x="0" y="380" width="1280" height="340" fill="url(#bottomBar)"/>
   204	```
   205	
   206	#### Radial Gradient Overlay — Vignette Effect
   207	
   208	Best for: full-screen atmosphere slides; draws attention to the center.
   209	
   210	```xml
   211	<defs>
   212	  <radialGradient id="vignette" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="70%">
   213	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   214	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.58"/>
   215	  </radialGradient>
   216	</defs>
   217	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#vignette)"/>
   218	```
   219	
   220	#### Brand Color Overlay
   221	
   222	Best for: slides needing strong visual brand identity.
   223	
   224	```xml
   225	<defs>
   226	  <linearGradient id="brandOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   227	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.80"/>
   228	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.10"/>
   229	  </linearGradient>
   230	</defs>
   231	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#brandOverlay)"/>
   232	```
   233	
   234	### Quick-Reference Table
   235	
   236	| Scenario | Recommended Technique | Avoid |
   237	|----------|-----------------------|-------|
   238	| Card / panel shadow | Filter soft shadow (`flood-opacity` ≤ 0.12) | Hard black shadow |
   239	| Accent / CTA button | Colored shadow (same hue family) | Generic gray shadow |
   240	| Text over image | Linear gradient overlay (direction matches text side) | Uniform flat opacity over whole image |
   241	| Cover / full-image slide | Bottom gradient bar + brand color | Solid black overlay |
   242	| Atmosphere / hero slide | Radial vignette | Unprocessed raw image |
   243	| Max PPT compatibility needed | Layered rect shadow | Filter-based shadow |

- **Layout**: Two-column (left: problem framing, right: data comparison)
- **Label**: MOTIVATION
- **Content points**:
  - State-of-the-art VLMs (Idefics-80B, Molmo-A1B-7B) require 27–80 GB GPU RAM

- **Layout**: Left-right split (image left, text right)
- **Label**: FINDING 3
- **Content points**:
  - Pixel shuffle rearranges spatial features into depth channels
  - Token reduction = r²: r=2 → 4× reduction; r=4 → 16× reduction

  - Performance improves significantly across all benchmarks with context extension
- **Visual**: Three cards with icon headers; timeline-style flow for context scaling

- **Layout**: Full-width data table + bottom RAM comparison bar
- **Label**: BENCHMARKS

  - Full 13-benchmark comparison table (Single-Image, Multi-task, Video)
  - Average scores: SmolVLM 256M 44.0% | 500M 51.0% | 2.2B 59.8%

  - SmolVLM-256M surpasses 300× larger Idefics-80B
- **Visual**: Structured data table (OCRBench, AI2D, ChartQA, TextVQA, DocVQA, ScienceQA, MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, Video-MME, MLVU); horizontal bar for RAM

- **Layout**: Top-bottom split (image top, metrics bottom)

  - SmolVLM-256M: ~80 tok/s on Pro M1 Max 64GB
  - Batch=64: nearly 1000 tok/s on high-end Apple Silicon
  - MacBook Air M3 16GB: ~55 tok/s
  - Throughput scales roughly linearly with batch size
- **Visual**: figure_2.jpg (mobile app + throughput) full width; 4 KPI cards below

- **Layout**: Dark background, 5 takeaway cards in grid
- **Label**: TAKEAWAYS
- **Content points**:
  1. **Balance encoder-LM compute** — smaller encoders win for compact LMs
  2. **Extend context length** — 2K→16K unlocks resolution and accuracy

    75	## Speaker Notes Style
    76	
    77	### Narrative Tone
    78	
    79	General style speaker notes use **conversational narration** — like talking with the audience, not reading a report. Natural tone with rhythm, using rhetorical devices where appropriate.
    80	
    81	### Stage Direction Markers
    82	
    83	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
    84	|--------|---------|---------|
    85	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key reveal, letting the audience absorb | "What does this number mean? [Pause] It means 1 in every 3 users..." |
    86	| `[Interactive]` | Ask questions or guide audience participation | "[Interactive] How many of you have used this feature?" |
    87	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Now that we understand the context, let's see how it works." |
    88	
    89	### Notes Writing Guidelines
    90	
    91	- **Tell stories**: Use "scenario-conflict-resolution" structure for each page's narrative
    92	- **Use metaphors**: Make abstract concepts tangible ("It's like adding a turbocharger to the system")
    93	- **Create suspense**: Pose questions at the right time, answer on the next page
    94	- **Conversational data**: 30% → "nearly one-third", 2.5x → "more than doubled"
    95	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core message (2) Supporting evidence (3) Call to action`
    96	
    97	### Notes Example
    98	
    99	```markdown
   100	# 03_key_advantages
   101	
   102	[Transition] Having covered the market landscape, you might be wondering: where is our opportunity?
   103	
   104	Our core advantages can be summed up in three words: Fast, Accurate, Efficient.
   105	Fast — deployment time cut from 3 months to 2 weeks; [Pause]
   106	Accurate — recognition accuracy at 97.3%, far exceeding the industry average of 82%;
   107	Efficient — overall costs reduced by nearly one-third.
   108	
   109	[Interactive] If you were the decision-maker, which of these three numbers would impress you most?
   110	
   111	Key points: (1) Three differentiating advantages (2) Quantitative data support (3) Prompt for reflection
   112	Duration: 2 minutes
   113	```

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to this technical presentation on SmolVLM, a family of compact vision-language models that redefine what is possible with efficient multimodal AI. SmolVLM is the result of a collaboration between Hugging Face and Stanford University, and it demonstrates that architectural efficiency can outperform raw scale by orders of magnitude.

[Pause] The key headline is right here: a 256-million parameter model running in under 1 GB of RAM that outperforms models 300 times larger. This is not incremental progress — it is a fundamental shift in how we design multimodal systems for the edge.

Key points: (1) SmolVLM is a family of compact VLMs from Hugging Face and Stanford (2) 256M model uses 0.8 GB RAM and surpasses Idefics-80B (3) All artifacts are fully open-sourced
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 02_problem

[Transition] Before diving into the architecture, let us frame the problem that SmolVLM was built to solve.

State-of-the-art vision-language models like Idefics-80B and Molmo-A1B-7B demand enormous GPU memory — 80 GB and 27.7 GB respectively. Meanwhile, the devices where multimodal AI would be most transformative — smartphones, tablets, edge cameras — operate with 4 to 8 GB of shared system memory. This creates a massive deployment gap between research benchmarks and real-world utility.

SmolVLM closes this gap with three model sizes: 256M for smartphones, 500M for mid-tier laptops, and 2.2B for high-end workstations. The smallest variant uses just 0.8 GB of RAM at batch size one, yet surpasses the 300-times-larger Idefics-80B model.

Key points: (1) SOTA VLMs require 27–80 GB GPU RAM (2) Edge devices constrained to 4–8 GB (3) SmolVLM-256M uses 0.8 GB and outperforms Idefics-80B
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture

[Transition] So how does SmolVLM achieve this? The answer lies in a carefully optimized pipeline with five stages.

First, input images are split into sub-images to handle high resolution without overwhelming the encoder. Second, a SigLIP vision encoder extracts patch-level features. Third, and this is critical, pixel shuffle performs space-to-depth compression, reducing the number of visual tokens by a factor of r squared. Fourth, a linear projection maps these compressed visual tokens into the SmolLM2 language model's input embedding space. Finally, they are concatenated with text token embeddings for autoregressive generation. For video, frames are sampled and processed through the identical pipeline.

Key points: (1) Five-stage pipeline: split → encode → compress → project → generate (2) Pixel shuffle is the critical efficiency lever (3) Video processed identically via frame sampling
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first major finding challenges conventional wisdom about vision encoder sizing.

One might assume that a larger vision encoder always improves performance. SmolVLM's experiments show the opposite for compact language models. A 93-million parameter SigLIP-B/16 paired with a 135-million parameter LM actually outperforms the 428-million parameter SigLIP-SO400M with the same LM. The smaller encoder prevents bottlenecking and allows the compact LM to operate more effectively. Only when the language model scales to approximately 1.7 billion parameters does the larger encoder justify its ten percent parameter overhead. This has immediate practical implications: for edge deployments, choose the smaller encoder.

Key points: (1) 93M encoder outperforms 428M encoder at small LM scales (2) Crossover point around 1.7B LM parameters (3) Practical implication: smaller encoders for edge deployment
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] Finding three concerns token compression via pixel shuffle — another counterintuitive result.

Pixel shuffle rearranges spatial features into depth channels. The reduction factor is r squared: r equals two gives four times reduction, while r equals four gives sixteen times reduction. Larger models prefer r equals two, but small VLMs actually benefit from the more aggressive r equals four compression. This is because small language models lack the capacity to attend effectively over thousands of visual tokens. By compressing sixteen-fold, we reduce attention overhead quadratically and enable better long-context modeling within the same memory budget.

Key points: (1) Pixel shuffle reduces tokens by r² (2) Small models prefer r=4 (16× reduction) (3) Reduces attention overhead, improves long-context modeling
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_context_length

[Transition] Finding two addresses context length — a dimension often overlooked in compact model design.

Performance improves significantly when extending context from two thousand to sixteen thousand tokens. This was achieved by scaling the RoPE position encoding base from ten thousand to two hundred seventy-three thousand, which extends effective position encodings twenty-seven-fold without aliasing. Critically, the model was fine-tuned on a mixture of long and short sequences to prevent degradation on short-context tasks. The 2.2-billion parameter model uses the full sixteen-thousand-token context, while the smaller variants use eight thousand tokens — a right-sized approach for their respective memory budgets.

Key points: (1) RoPE base 10K → 273K enables 16K context (2) Mixed long/short fine-tuning prevents degradation (3) Model-specific context: 16K for 2.2B, 8K for smaller variants
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmarks

[Transition] Let us look at the numbers. SmolVLM was evaluated across thirteen benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension.

The full table shows consistent gains across all model sizes. Averages are forty-four percent for the 256-million model, fifty-one percent for the 500-million, and fifty-nine point eight percent for the 2.2-billion. The 2.2-billion model rivals or exceeds the best efficient open-source baselines — Molmo-A1B-7B and InternVL2-2B — while using a fraction of the memory. Most striking is the RAM comparison: SmolVLM ranges from zero point eight to four point nine gigabytes, while Molmo requires twenty-seven point seven gigabytes. The 256-million model surpasses the three-hundred-times-larger Idefics-80B.

Key points: (1) Averages: 44.0% / 51.0% / 59.8% (2) RAM: 0.8–4.9 GB vs. Molmo 27.7 GB (3) 256M surpasses 300× larger Idefics-80B
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 08_on_device

[Transition] Benchmarks are one thing. Real-world deployment is another. SmolVLM runs entirely on-device via the HuggingSnap iOS application.

All inference is local — zero cloud dependency, zero network latency, full privacy. Throughput on Apple Silicon is impressive: approximately eighty tokens per second on a Pro M1 Max, and nearly one thousand tokens per second at batch size sixty-four on high-end devices. Even on an entry-level MacBook Air M3 with sixteen gigabytes of memory, the 256-million model achieves roughly fifty-five tokens per second. Throughput scales roughly linearly with batch size for the smallest model, making it ideal for batched edge workloads.

Key points: (1) HuggingSnap iOS app: 100% local inference (2) ~80 tok/s on Pro M1 Max; ~1000 tok/s at batch=64 (3) ~55 tok/s on MacBook Air M3 16GB
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 09_takeaways

[Transition] To conclude, SmolVLM delivers five actionable design principles for efficient multimodal models.

First, balance encoder-LM compute: smaller encoders win for compact language models. Second, extend context length: scaling from two thousand to sixteen thousand tokens unlocks resolution and accuracy. Third, use aggressive token compression: r equals four for small models, r equals two for large. Fourth, sub-one-gigabyte inference is achievable and competitive. Fifth, fully open-source releases accelerate the entire field. The overarching lesson is this: architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale. When every design choice is optimized for the target deployment environment, small models can punch far above their weight.

Key points: (1) Five design principles for efficient VLMs (2) Architectural efficiency > raw scale (3) All artifacts open-sourced to advance on-device AI research
Duration: 2 minutes
